title: Ashtpadi 3, salok: many scriptures
hook: I have searched many scriptures; none equals the Name (Sukhmani 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sang, and your line: never alone. Today, the third ashtpadi opens with its salok.

Shelves to the ceiling. Notes in every margin. A reader with an answer to every question you could ask. A person like that can teach a great deal. And then there's the other kind: someone who has read very little, yet carries a steadiness the reader doesn't. A grandmother who knew three prayers by heart and lived every one of them. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Arjan, the author of Sukhmani, as the Guru who gathered the hymns of the Adi Granth. And the third ashtpadi opens with a surprising thing for a compiler of scripture to say.
screen: `SHELVES TO THE CEILING.` → `A GRANDMOTHER WITH THREE PRAYERS.` → `A COMPILER OF SCRIPTURE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol. Word by word. Bahu: many. Saasatr: the shastras, the learned treatises of Guru Arjan's world. Simritee: the smritis, the remembered law-books and traditions. Pekhe: I have looked at. Sarab dhadhol: searched through them all. Then the second line: poojas naahee har hare, Naanak naam amol. In paraphrase: they do not equal God, Har, Har; Nanak, the Name is priceless. Amol means beyond price, something no money could buy. Notice who's speaking. Not someone who dismisses books without opening them. Someone who says, I have looked, I've searched them all: a scholar, not a scorner. And what he found is that the books point beyond themselves. Learning can describe the Name, but it can't be the Name. Read this way, the salok isn't against study. The Guru Granth Sahib is itself a book, and Sikhs read from it and sing from it. The salok is about the difference between knowing about God and remembering God. Learning about water is not drinking it. Some readers hear the line as just as true of their own scripture: reading the Guru Granth Sahib without remembering the One it points to would miss the point too. Over the next days, the third ashtpadi's stanzas run through a long list of religious efforts, and set each beside the Name.
screen: `BAHU SAASATR: MANY SCRIPTURES.` · `I HAVE SEARCHED THEM ALL.` · `AMOL: BEYOND PRICE.` · `KNOWING ABOUT VS. REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `NOTHING EQUALS THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Choose one line you know, from Sukhmani, from Japji, or from anything that matters to you; if nothing comes, use this: Nanak, the Name is priceless. Say it once at normal speed, then at half speed, then one word per breath, and let the last word rest. If you pray, add Waheguru.
Amol, priceless: Sukhmani's third section, whose salok says, I have searched many shastras and smritis, and none equals God; Nanak, the Name is priceless.
Your line: nothing equals the name. He searched them all, and came back to the Name. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the third ashtpadi; Sikh teachers cite it when speaking of the difference between scholarship and lived remembrance of the Name.

fork.setup: you've searched every learned treatise and law-book of your day. what does the third salok say you find?
options: that none of them equals God, and the Name is priceless.
fork.reveal: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol: searched them all, and the Name is amol, beyond price.

original.note: Gurmukhi: amol, priceless; the salok's last word for the Name.

trapdoor: what you thought: many scriptures means reading widely.
what it means: the salok's speaker has searched every shastra and smriti and found that none equals remembering God.
what a scholar hears: saasatr and simritee name the Sanskrit learned and legal corpora; the salok contrasts textual knowledge with naam, without rejecting study.
guess: priceless, beyond what money could buy
rare, found only in old scripture
heavy, too weighty to lift alone

chat.says: Is that Sukhmani salok telling people to stop reading scripture?
options: No: Guru Arjan says he searched them all; the books point beyond themselves to the Name.
Yes: it says any time spent reading holy books is wasted, so Sikhs shouldn't study.
No: it says the Name can only be found by those who have read every scripture.
chat.meaning: The speaker has searched many shastras and smritis; the point is knowing about God versus remembering God. The Name is amol, priceless.

shastras.meaning: the learned treatises of Guru Arjan's world

Adi Granth.meaning: the scripture Guru Arjan gathered, later the Guru Granth Sahib

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's morning prayer, first in the scripture

Salok transliterated 'bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol / poojas naahee har hare naanak naam amol' with glosses; confirm, especially dhadhol (searched through).
Framing: the salok is presented as about knowing vs remembering, applied by Sikhs to their own scripture too, to avoid any ranking of other traditions' texts. Confirm a Keeper agrees.
